abstract: HLA associations are among the strongest genetic risk factors in immune-mediated disease, yet they rarely explain incomplete penetrance, tissue localization, or opposing effects of different alleles. We use T cell-mediated drug hypersensitivity and multiple sclerosis as complementary mechanistic anchors. Drug hypersensitivity shows that a defined exposure can create or alter a peptide-HLA surface and may recruit pre-existing class I-restricted memory in some early reactions, while allowing naive-derived responses in others. Patch-confirmed abacavir reactions beginning as early as 36 h, together with responses in drug-unexposed HLA-B*57:01 carriers, are difficult to reconcile with obligatory de novo naive priming in every case; in other drug hypersensitivity reactions the relative contributions of memory- and naive-derived cells to clinical injury remain unresolved. Multiple sclerosis adds a lifelong antigen source and separates HLA-DRB1*15:01-associated class II specificity from class I associations with measured Epstein-Barr virus burden and from candidate tissue execution. Together, these systems separate three HLA functions: specificity and focusing, antigen-source control, and tissue execution; and three temporal stages: imprinting and licensing, tissue recall, and local amplification. For T-cell receptor-mediated injury, we propose interacting requirements involving receptor-HLA compatibility, functional ligand and abundance, natural tissue presentation, and local regulation. Within this general architecture, Keystone Epitope Theory proposes that persistent, human-adapted organisms exert disproportionate influence on durable immune memory. That memory-source hypothesis is independently testable and is not a prerequisite for the broader framework. We distinguish antigenic target recognition from inflammatory amplification and propose a lesion-anchored, receptor-first experimental strategy with explicit disconfirming outcomes. Predictive-value calculations distinguish clinical screening decisions from mechanistic inference and show how measured modifiers can motivate competing, experimentally testable causal models.
